identity.title: Characterizing the Discrete Geometry of ReLU Networks

problem.claim: Characterize the discrete geometry of the polyhedral linear-region complexes induced by fully connected ReLU networks.

gap.claim: Beyond total-region-count bounds, little is known about the geometry of these complexes, and exact calculation is generally intractable.

contributions.claim: Proves results for connectivity graphs whose nodes are regions and whose edges join regions sharing a face, applying to all fully connected ReLU networks.
Establishes an average-degree upper bound of twice the input dimension, independent of network width and depth, and a diameter upper bound independent of input dimension.
Reports experiments on networks trained with synthetic and real-world data to provide additional geometric insight.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish the work by providing new theoretical results about ReLU-region connectivity complexes for all fully connected networks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that average graph degree is at most twice the input dimension regardless of width and depth.

The authors report a dimension-independent diameter upper bound despite exponentially increasing region counts with input dimension, and say experiments on synthetic and real-world data corroborate the findings.
The authors provide code intended to reproduce their results.

narrative_sequence.summary: ReLU networks induce continuous piecewise-linear functions whose polyhedral regions partition input space.
Because nonlinearities occur at region boundaries, how regions connect is behaviorally important, yet geometric understanding is limited and exact computation is usually intractable.
The work studies connectivity graphs of regions and derives graph-theoretic bounds valid for fully connected ReLU networks.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world trained networks are reported as additional geometric support and insight.
A code repository is provided for reproducing the reported results.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a local structural quantity (average graph degree) to input dimension while explicitly noting independence from width and depth, and separately states a diameter bound independent of input dimension.

lessons.interpretation: Separating which architectural variables a bound depends on can make a theoretical claim more informative than reporting a single complexity measure.
lessons.application: When presenting a new network-geometry result, state each bound together with explicit dependence and independence on architecture and input variables.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the omitted variables are essential to the theorem or when the abstract cannot establish the relevant independence.

unknowns: The abstract does not state the exact diameter bound, theorem assumptions beyond fully connected ReLU networks, or proof details.
Experimental architectures, datasets, metrics, baselines, and quantitative results are not specified, so the extent of corroboration cannot be assessed from the abstract.
